nodes.title: Beta
nodes.body:
# Beta

**In one sentence:** Beta measures how much a stock moves compared to the overall market.

## Notes
- Learned how to calculate it on .

> [!info] Added by Claude
> **Formula**
> $$\beta = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_m)}{\text{Var}(R_m)}$$
> - $R_i$ = the stock's returns, $R_m$ = the market's returns (usually the S&P 500)
> - Same thing as the **slope** when you regress the stock's returns on the market's returns
>
> **How to read it**
> | Beta | Meaning |
> |---|---|
> | β = 1 | Moves with the market |
> | β > 1 | More volatile than the market (e.g. 1.5 → ~15% move when market moves 10%) |
> | 0 < β < 1 | Less volatile than the market |
> | β < 0 | Tends to move opposite to the market |
>
> **In Excel/Sheets:** `=SLOPE(stock_returns, market_returns)` or `=COVARIANCE.S(stock, market)/VAR.S(market)`
>
> Beta only captures (market-wide risk), not risk specific to one company. It's the key input to the .

nodes.title: Market Risk Premium
nodes.body:
# Market Risk Premium

**In one sentence:** Market Risk Premium is NOT the same thing as market expected return.

## Notes
- Easy to mix these up. ⚠️

> [!info] Added by Claude
> **Market Risk Premium (MRP) = Expected market return − Risk-free rate**
> $$MRP = E(R_m) - R_f$$
> - **Market expected return** $E(R_m)$ = the *total* return you expect from the market (e.g. 10%)
> - **Market risk premium** = only the *extra* return on top of the risk-free rate, as a reward for taking risk (e.g. 10% − 4% = 6%)
>
> **Why it matters:** In the , you multiply [[Beta]] by the **premium**, not the total return:
> $$E(R_i) = R_f + \beta \times (E(R_m) - R_f)$$
> Common mistake: using $E(R_m)$ where the formula needs $E(R_m) - R_f$. That double-counts the risk-free rate.
>
> **Watch the wording in problems:** "the market's expected return is 10%" → subtract $R_f$ yourself. "The market risk premium is 6%" → plug it in directly.
